Red blood cells in hyperadrenalinemia

One rat experiment found no immediate red-cell change but reported partial normalization of several measures after 24 hours. There is no clinical evidence that PBM improves red-cell function in people with hyperadrenalinemia.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One rat experiment found no immediate red-cell change but reported partial normalization of several measures after 24 hours. There is no clinical evidence that PBM improves red-cell function in people with hyperadrenalinemia.

Summary of the Evidence

One publication directly addresses red-cell changes during hyperadrenalinemia. It is a rat experiment filed within the broader red-blood-cell category. The larger category contains laboratory studies of red cells under other conditions, but those are not counted here because they do not test adrenaline-associated changes. No separate clinical trial or independent replication of this exact model was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No study in the indication set has tested PBM in people with hyperadrenalinemia or measured whether treatment improves symptoms or clinical outcomes. The findings below are limited to experimental blood measures in rats.

Animal evidence

In rats given adrenaline, laser treatment did not significantly change red-cell measures one hour later. At 24 hours, the authors reported fewer abnormal red-cell forms, changes in cell-shape patterns, higher electrophoretic mobility and osmotic resistance, and a red-cell count closer to that in untreated healthy animals. These outcomes suggest a delayed change in the model, but the result comes from one experiment and has not established a treatment effect in patients (Deryugina et al. 2019).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or ex-vivo publication directly modeled adrenaline-associated red-cell changes. Broader laboratory studies of red-cell responses are adjacent evidence and cannot independently confirm the hyperadrenalinemia result.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The rat study used 890-nm near-infrared light for a ten-minute exposure. The database does not provide a sufficiently clear dose description to compare it with other red-cell experiments. No comparison of wavelengths or dose levels was reported for this indication. A single animal exposure cannot define a human treatment protocol.

Interpretation

The study reports delayed improvement in selected rat blood measures, but it does not establish a reproducible effect or a health benefit for people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for adrenaline-associated red-cell changes in rats
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

This rating reflects one rat experiment with delayed changes in red-cell shape and physical properties, without independent replication or patient outcomes. A repeat study with prespecified blood measures and a clearly reported light dose would test whether the result is reproducible. Any stronger clinical claim would then require human studies showing that the laboratory changes correspond to a health benefit.
